did_you_know.text: Did you know? Job calls his friends “miserable comforters”—that is, comforters whose words add trouble and sorrow instead of bringing comfort.
Did you know? Job asks how long his friends will go on speaking and compares their words to “words of wind”—meaning, in his view, useless talk.
Did you know? Job uses a role reversal as an example: if his friends were in his place, he could speak to them in the same way they speak to him.
Did you know? Job says that if he were speaking to his friends, he would try to strengthen them, highlighting the difference between true comfort and words of criticism.
Did you know? Job presents his pain as something that does not lessen through either speaking or remaining silent: “If I speak … or refrain”—in either case, he remains in distress.
Did you know? Job describes his shrunken, emaciated body as having become, in his words, “a witness” against him; his body itself becomes part of the picture of his suffering.
Did you know? In describing how those around him treat him, Job uses images of humiliation and violence: open mouths, disgrace, and striking on the cheek.
Did you know? Job describes mourning practices: he sews sackcloth onto his skin and brings his horn—meaning his honor or stature—down to the dust.
Did you know? Alongside his description of suffering, Job claims his innocence: there is no violence in his hands, and his prayer is pure.
Did you know? Although Job feels abandoned, he declares that he has a witness and a testimony in heaven, in the heights.
